headline: GTA VI launches to record-breaking 39M players, sending Take-Two surging 5.9% — meanwhile the ASX had a cracking session, up 1.8%, while the Middle East conflict escalates with Houthi strikes on Riyadh.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: GTA VI launched on PlayStation to record-breaking numbers — 39 million unique players and the biggest PlayStation launch in history. The market loved it. Shares surged ~5.9% last night as investors priced in the monster commercial success of the game Take-Two has been building toward for years.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: A strong day for AI and semiconductor stocks globally lifted GXAI today. Reports of a sharp rebound in semiconductor stocks (the SOXX index headed for its biggest single-day gain in 18+ months) dragged AI-focused ETFs higher across the board.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: Emerging market stocks had a strong session today, with the ETF jumping 3.5%. A broadly positive risk-on mood across Asian and EM markets provided the lift — no single country catalyst, just broad-based buying.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS tracks the entire US share market and rose 2.8% in today's ASX session, riding the tailwind from recent strength in US equities. Note that the US market itself fell last night (NASDAQ -1.7%), so today's ASX price partially reflects currency and prior US session moves.

movers.name: DHHF (BetaShares Diversified All Growth ETF)
movers.note: DHHF holds a broad mix of global and Australian shares and rose 2.2% today as the ASX rallied strongly. It tracks global markets, so the strong ASX 200 session was the main driver.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG rose nearly 2% today, lifted by the strong ASX session. It holds a diversified basket of Australian and international shares, so broad market strength pulls it higher. Long-term thesis remains solid.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft edged up 0.4% last night after recently beating earnings estimates and lifting its dividend. It's holding steady near recent highs — the AI cloud story continues to attract buyers and the stock is in decent shape.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara slipped another 0.7% today. The lithium price remains stubbornly weak — even China's electric truck boom hasn't been enough to lift lithium demand meaningfully, with oversupply still weighing heavily on the sector.

movers.name: Alphabet (Google)
movers.note: GOOG fell 1.4% last night, giving back some of the big 7% gain it posted earlier in the week after strong quarterly earnings and 103% growth in Google Cloud. This looks like profit-taking after a sharp run-up — the underlying business results were very strong.

watch_today.title: GTA VI launch: Take-Two's big moment — hold and enjoy
watch_today.detail: GTA VI has launched to 39 million unique players and broken PlayStation launch records. Take-Two surged 5.9% last night and is now sitting on a 2.7% overall gain for you. This is exactly what long-term holders were waiting for — the thesis has played out. No reason to sell into excitement; hold and let the game's commercial success continue to flow through.

watch_today.title: GOOG dip after strong earnings — sit tight
watch_today.detail: Google fell 1.4% last night but that's just profit-taking after a 7% surge on stellar earnings (Google Cloud grew 103%). The business is firing on all cylinders. You're down ~10% overall on this position, but the long-term story — AI, cloud, search — is as strong as ever. Nothing to do here but hold.

watch_today.title: PLS continues to bleed — the lithium pain isn't over
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals slipped another 0.7% today and you're now down nearly 60% on this position. The core problem hasn't changed: lithium is oversupplied globally, and even surging EV demand in China (electric trucks booming) hasn't moved the price. This is a structural issue, not short-term noise. Worth seriously asking whether the thesis still holds — if you believe in a lithium recovery in 2-3 years, hold; if not, review.

watch_today.title: GXAI bouncing — but still deep in the red overall
watch_today.detail: GXAI had a great day today, up 4.4%, riding a sharp global semiconductor and AI stock rebound. But you're still down 19% overall on this position. The AI infrastructure story is real and long-term, so there's no reason to panic — but be aware this ETF can be volatile. Hold and let the theme play out.

watch_today.title: RBA rate cut expectations building — good for your ETFs
watch_today.detail: Multiple banks are now tipping RBA rate cuts — ANZ sees June 2027, while some forecasters are picking cuts even sooner. Lower rates tend to be a tailwind for share markets, especially growth-oriented ETFs like VDHG and DHHF. Nothing to act on today, but the broader environment is tilting more favourably for equities.

watch_today.title: Middle East conflict escalating — oil price to watch
watch_today.detail: Houthis struck a skyscraper in Riyadh's financial district, and the Strait of Hormuz is reportedly nearly paralysed with 400 ships waiting. Oil (WTI) has jumped over 2% to $81.81. If this escalates further, oil prices could spike meaningfully, which flows through to inflation and potentially delays rate cuts globally.

world.summary: The Middle East conflict is escalating sharply, with Houthi rebels striking central Riyadh and the Strait of Hormuz under pressure. Meanwhile, a break-in at Prince William and Kate's country home and broader questions about the US military's repositioning in the region round out a busy day globally.

stories.title: Houthis strike Riyadh financial centre tower, Strait of Hormuz nearly paralysed
stories.why_it_matters: Yemen's Houthi rebels launched a missile strike on a skyscraper in Riyadh's financial district, injuring 11 people. Separately, the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow waterway through which about 20% of the world's oil passes — is reportedly virtually paralysed, with around 400 ships sitting and waiting. If the strait remains blocked or restricted, it would put serious upward pressure on oil prices globally, which means higher fuel and energy costs for everyday Australians.

stories.title: How the Iran war is reshaping the US military presence in the Middle East
stories.why_it_matters: The ongoing conflict involving Iran is forcing the US to rethink how and where it stations military assets across the Middle East. The US is reportedly repositioning forces in response to the broader regional war, which signals this conflict is not winding down. For markets, a prolonged Middle East war means sustained oil price pressure and ongoing uncertainty for global trade routes.

stories.title: Israeli official says no immediate Iran threat requiring military action
stories.why_it_matters: Israeli National Security Council member Eisenkot said publicly that Israel does not currently see an immediate Iranian threat that requires a military response. This is a small but meaningful signal that the conflict may not escalate to a direct Israel-Iran exchange right now — which matters for anyone watching oil prices and regional stability. It doesn't mean the situation is calm, but it lowers the chance of an immediate major escalation.

stories.title: Two men arrested after breaking into Prince William and Kate's country home
stories.why_it_matters: Two men broke into the country home of Prince William and Princess Kate and were arrested on the property. No details yet on who they were or what their intentions were, but it highlights ongoing security concerns around the Royal Family. The incident occurred in the UK and is under investigation.

stories.title: 2026 Economic Outlook: AI boom and post-election landscape under the microscope
stories.why_it_matters: The University of Chicago is convening its 2026 Economic Outlook forum to examine two big forces shaping the global economy: the AI investment boom and the shifting political landscape after recent US elections. Economists are trying to figure out whether the massive AI spending wave will translate into real productivity gains, or whether it's getting ahead of itself — a question that's very relevant to anyone holding AI-related stocks.

markets.summary: The ASX had a strong session today, up 1.8% to close at 8,726. All major ASX holdings finished well in the green. Last night in the US, the NASDAQ dropped 1.7% and the S&P 500 fell 0.7% — tech stocks gave back some recent gains. Oil is up 2% on Middle East tensions, while gold slid 2.6% as risk appetite returned.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Strong session today — broad-based buying across the market.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Last night's session — modest pullback after recent highs.

indicators.name: NASDAQ
indicators.note: Last night — tech stocks sold off, giving back some gains.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Rising on Middle East tensions and Strait of Hormuz disruption.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Fell as risk appetite returned and investors moved into equities.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: Barely moved — Aussie dollar holding steady around 66.4 US cents.

politics.summary: Foreign Minister Penny Wong is pushing back on Labor critics urging Australia to distance itself from the US under Trump, Treasurer Jim Chalmers is warning of tougher economic times ahead, and new online safety laws targeting doomscrolling are close to passing with Greens support.

stories.title: Wong warns Labor: Australia cannot abandon the US despite Trump turmoil
stories.why_it_matters: Foreign Minister Penny Wong is pushing back against voices within Labor who think Australia should cool its relationship with the US given Donald Trump's unpredictable foreign policy. Wong's argument is that Australia can't simply walk away from its most important security alliance — even if it disagrees with specific US policies. This debate matters because how Australia navigates the US relationship under Trump will shape defence spending, trade policy and our standing in the region.

stories.title: Chalmers warns unemployment to surpass 5% and 'things will get harder'
stories.why_it_matters: Treasurer Jim Chalmers has issued a candid warning: unemployment is expected to rise above 5% and economic conditions are going to get harder before they improve. He also flagged spending cuts ahead of the mid-year budget update (MYEFO). For everyday Australians, this means a tougher job market and potentially tighter government services — though Chalmers framed it as a necessary reset to get the budget back on track.

stories.title: RBA rate cuts tipped by mid-2027 — banks divided on timing
stories.why_it_matters: ANZ is forecasting the RBA's first interest rate cut won't come until June 2027, while other analysts are tipping cuts could arrive sooner. The RBA (Australia's central bank) has been holding rates high to fight inflation. Rate cuts matter a lot for mortgage holders — a cut of 0.25% on a typical $600k mortgage saves roughly $90-$100 a month. The debate now is whether Chalmers' planned spending cuts will give the RBA enough comfort to move earlier.

stories.title: Digital Duty of Care bill nears law with Labor-Greens deal — doomscrolling in the crosshairs
stories.why_it_matters: Labor and the Greens have struck a deal to pass the Digital Duty of Care legislation, which would legally require tech platforms (think Instagram, TikTok, YouTube) to consider addictive design features like doomscrolling (endlessly scrolling through feeds) in how they build their products. Companies that fail to protect users — especially kids — from harmful addictive patterns could face legal consequences. Critics are raising free speech concerns, arguing the laws are too broad.

ai.summary: AI safety concerns are dominating the headlines today — insiders at OpenAI and Anthropic are reportedly worried about unreleased models being too dangerous to launch. Meanwhile, regulators globally are stepping up scrutiny of autonomous AI agents, and Australia is debating what role it should play in global AI governance.

stories.title: OpenAI and Anthropic staff fear some unreleased AI models are too risky to ship
stories.why_it_matters: Employees at both OpenAI (maker of ChatGPT) and Anthropic (maker of Claude) are reportedly raising internal alarms that some of the AI models being developed are too dangerous to release publicly. This is significant because it suggests the companies themselves are hitting capability thresholds that make even insiders uncomfortable. It also adds weight to calls for stronger AI regulation — both companies are racing to stay ahead of each other, but their own staff are pumping the brakes.

stories.title: UK financial regulator warns: autonomous AI agents may trigger financial laws
stories.why_it_matters: The UK's Financial Conduct Authority has put tech firms on notice: if your AI agents (programs that can take actions on their own, like making trades or managing accounts) operate in financial markets, they could be subject to financial services regulation. This is a world first in terms of regulatory framing and signals that autonomous AI — not just AI tools used by humans — is now firmly on regulators' radar. For anyone using AI in investing or financial planning, this is a space to watch.

stories.title: Australia should be securing rules and power over AI safety — Capital Brief
stories.why_it_matters: An analysis piece today argues Australia is falling behind in the global AI governance race and needs to both set rules and build real influence over how AI develops internationally. The argument is that countries that shape AI safety frameworks will have more power over how the technology is deployed globally — and Australia risks being a rule-taker rather than a rule-maker if it doesn't move faster.

stories.title: Ant Group's AI app open sources a medical and health AI model family
stories.why_it_matters: Ant Group — the fintech giant behind Alipay — has open-sourced a family of AI models specifically trained for medical and health applications through its AI app Afu. Open-sourcing means anyone can use and build on these models for free. It's a significant move that could accelerate AI-powered healthcare tools globally, particularly in areas where specialised medical AI was previously only available to well-funded companies.

sport.summary: The NRL Grand Final is done — Roosters beat the Knights 19-18 in a thriller at Accor Stadium. In transfer news, Cameron Munster has knocked back an offer, sending the NRL into a frenzy. World No.1 tennis player Jannik Sinner faces knee surgery and could miss the Australian Open.

stories.title: Roosters beat Knights 19-18 in NRL Grand Final thriller
stories.why_it_matters: The Sydney Roosters have claimed the 2026 NRL premiership, defeating the Newcastle Knights 19-18 in an absolute nail-biter at Accor Stadium. One point in it at the final siren — it doesn't get closer than that. The Knights will be gutted having come so close to their first title in years, while the Roosters add another premiership to their storied history.

stories.title: Cameron Munster rejects offer — NRL in a frenzy
stories.why_it_matters: Cameron Munster has knocked back an offer — the report doesn't specify from which club — sending the NRL player market into a frenzy. Munster is one of the most exciting and sought-after players in the competition, so his decision on where he plays next will have major ripple effects on rival clubs' rosters and salary caps. More details expected in coming days.

stories.title: PNG Chiefs spending scrutinised as new NRL franchise takes shape
stories.why_it_matters: SMH has crunched the numbers on the PNG Chiefs' signings ahead of their NRL debut, raising questions about whether the new franchise is spending wisely. The Chiefs have already locked in England international AJ Brimson on a three-year deal and signed former Raiders players to 'shape the culture'. The analysis questions whether the salary cap spend is being allocated to the right positions — a critical issue for a brand new club trying to be competitive from day one.

stories.title: Jannik Sinner faces knee surgery — Australian Open participation in doubt
stories.why_it_matters: World No.1 Jannik Sinner has undergone knee surgery and could miss the Australian Open in January 2027 — with some reports suggesting he might not return until Wimbledon in June. Sinner has dominated men's tennis this year and his absence from Melbourne Park would be a massive blow to the tournament's drawcard power. Australian Open organisers and tennis fans alike will be watching his recovery closely.
